claims.text: The patient presented to the emergency department on 05/01/26 with sudden severe central chest pain rated 8/10, described as sharp and exacerbated by deep breaths and movement, with an onset approximately one hour prior to arrival.
Associated symptoms included mild shortness of breath, while the patient denied haemoptysis, nausea, vomiting, palpitations, syncope, dysphagia, dysuria, haematuria, dizziness, or focal weakness.
Past medical history includes asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis, with a known allergy to pollen.
Social history indicates the patient lives alone, is independent with activities of daily living, works as an IT consultant, and is a non-smoker with no alcohol or recreational drug use.
The patient reported no current medications at the time of presentation.
Initial observations on 05/01/26 at 02:10 recorded a heart rate of 110 bpm, blood pressure of 135/85 mmHg, respiratory rate of 24/min, temperature of 37.1°C, and oxygen saturation of 96% on room air.
Physical examination on 05/01/26 revealed mild tenderness over the sternum and palpable subcutaneous crepitus in the neck and anterior chest wall, with equal air entry and no added breath sounds.
An ECG performed at 02:30 on 05/01/26 showed sinus tachycardia with no ischaemic changes.
A chest X-ray performed on 05/01/26 at 02:50 demonstrated subcutaneous emphysema and pneumomediastinum without evidence of pneumothorax.
The clinical diagnosis was spontaneous pneumomediastinum, likely secondary to a recent coughing episode or straining, with the patient accepted for admission to the respiratory high-dependency unit.

Initial management on 05/01/26 included conservative measures, paracetamol 1g four times daily for pain, and ibuprofen 400mg three times daily for pain, with advice to avoid straining or heavy lifting.

A physiotherapy session on 05/01/26 at 11:00 recorded a heart rate of 88 bpm, blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg, respiratory rate of 20/min, and oxygen saturation of 96% on room air, with the patient demonstrating reduced accessory muscle use.
Physiotherapy intervention on 05/01/26 included guided diaphragmatic breathing and pursed-lip breathing exercises, with education on avoiding activities that increase intrathoracic pressure.

On review on 05/01/26, observations showed a heart rate of 88 bpm, blood pressure of 130/80 mmHg, respiratory rate of 18/min, and oxygen saturation of 97% on room air, with examination noting no subcutaneous emphysema and no respiratory distress.
Omeprazole 20mg once daily was initiated on 05/01/26 to prevent gastrointestinal side effects from ibuprofen.
A repeat chest X-ray on 06/01/26 showed a slight reduction in pneumomediastinum compared to initial imaging.

A physiotherapy session on 06/01/26 at 12:00 recorded a heart rate of 88 bpm, blood pressure of 130/80 mmHg, respiratory rate of 18/min, and oxygen saturation of 97% on room air, with subcutaneous emphysema noted but no evidence of spread.
On 07/01/26, the patient reported no chest pain overnight and mild improvement in breathing comfort, with examination showing no palpable subcutaneous crepitus.
Regular paracetamol and ibuprofen were discontinued on 07/01/26 as the patient was pain-free.
On 07/01/26, the patient received education regarding signs of pneumomediastinum recurrence and when to seek urgent medical attention post-discharge.

On 08/01/26, observations recorded a heart rate of 82 bpm, blood pressure of 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate of 16/min, temperature of 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation of 97% on air, with examination showing no subcutaneous crepitus and clear chest.
A chest X-ray on 08/01/26 showed stable pneumomediastinum with no complications.
On 08/01/26 at 11:15, the ward nurse contacted the patient's GP to inform them of the patient's clinical progress and stability in preparation for discharge planning.
A final chest X-ray reviewed on 09/01/26 demonstrated complete resolution of spontaneous pneumomediastinum with no subcutaneous emphysema or abnormalities.
Discharge was planned for 10/01/26 with routine outpatient follow-up in the respiratory clinic arranged, and no further imaging was required.
